title: Who was the original "goodfella"? | CRIME WORDS

entries.note: From a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to sieve, sifting degrees of legality or morality; in 13th-century English it implied sinfulness more than unlawfulness.
An Anglo-Saxon legal term that sounds brutal next to French ones, discussed in an earlier episode; unlike [[see:murder]], it does not imply premeditation.
An Old English word used for a wrongdoing before English took [[see:crime]] from French.
Another Old English word that meant a crime.
Means completely crooked, from a Latin word [[from:pravus]] meaning crooked.
From Latin [[from:via]], way or road; a deviant is one who strays off the figurative moral path.
One of Jess's favourite roots, meaning way or road, found in [[gave:deviant]], [[gave:obvious]] and [[gave:impervious]].
Something obvious is immediately in your path, from Latin [[from:via]].
Something impervious has no way through it, from Latin [[from:via]].
To not have your life in order, the opposite of [[from:behave]].
The intensifying prefix [[from:be-]] plus have: to really have yourself together.
A workhorse prefix that can remove things, turn nouns into verbs of mistreatment or intensify, as in [[see:behead]], [[see:bedevil]], [[see:betongue]] and [[gave:behave]].
An example of the prefix [[from:be-]] removing something.
An example of [[from:be-]] turning a noun into a verb of doing terrible things to people.
An example of the intensifier [[from:be-]], meaning to attack someone verbally.
An old word for misbehaviour or criminal behaviour; you could commit an abusion.
An old word for criminal behaviour, with the same bode as [[same-root:forbode]], related to [[same-root:bid]] and [[same-root:bade]].
Contains the same bode as [[same-root:misbode]].
Related to [[same-root:misbode]], discussed in an earlier episode.
Related to [[same-root:misbode]], discussed in an earlier episode.
Implies malice and premeditation, unlike [[see:manslaughter]]; from Old English [[from:murther]], cognate with Old Norse [[same-root:morð]], from a root meaning to rub away or die.
A secret slaying, a more heinous crime than [[see:víg]]; cognate with [[same-root:murder]].
Old Norse for regular old killing, less heinous than [[see:morð]].
The Old English precursor of [[gave:murder]].
Shares the root of [[same-root:murder]], meaning to rub away or die.
Shares the root of [[same-root:murder]], meaning to rub away or die.
Shares the root of [[same-root:murder]], meaning to rub away or die.
Literally a dead pledge, because the deal dies when the property is paid off or seized, not because you pay until death; related to [[same-root:murder]].
A collective noun from the 15th-century Book of St Albans, reflecting crows' behaviour and association with bad omens.
One of the collective nouns in the Book of St Albans alongside [[see:murder of crows]].
One of the collective nouns in the Book of St Albans alongside [[see:murder of crows]].
One of the collective nouns in the Book of St Albans alongside [[see:murder of crows]].
A collective noun for people in the Book of St Albans, kinder to lawyers than most historical names for them.
Another collective noun for people in the Book of St Albans, a play on [[see:sentence]].
Related to [[same-root:sentiment]], [[same-root:sense]] and [[same-root:sensitive]]: a judge's sentence is an opinion handed down, not a reference to finality.
Related to [[same-root:sentence]] through the idea of a feeling or opinion.
Related to [[same-root:sentence]] through the idea of a feeling or opinion.
Related to [[same-root:sentence]] through the idea of a feeling or opinion.
An ending for killing found in about 50 English words, from [[gave:homicide]] and [[gave:regicide]] to [[gave:pulicide]] and [[gave:verbicide]].
Basically to cut off an argument in order to reach a conclusion, one of the [[see:-cide]] words.
One of the unusual [[see:-cide]] words for killing.
A general word for killing a parent, without specifying [[see:patricide]] or [[see:matricide]].
The killing of a father, a more specific word than [[see:parricide]].
The killing of a mother, a more specific word than [[see:parricide]].
The killing of a flea, one of the unusual [[see:-cide]] words.
The killing of a prophet, one of the unusual [[see:-cide]] words.
The killing of a god, one of the unusual [[see:-cide]] words.
One of the few [[see:-cide]] words we actually hear about regularly.
One of the few [[see:-cide]] words we actually hear about regularly.
The killing of a king, one of the commoner [[see:-cide]] words.
Distorting a word's meaning through misuse until it's meaningless, which misinformation and disinformation do a lot today.
The killing of a language, which has happened to many Indigenous languages through conquest and colonialism.
A rare Old English–Latin hybrid: the Normans added a Latinate ending to [[from:burh]] from [[from:burhbrecere]]; it means breaking in rather than stealing.
A purely American and fairly recent verb; British English uses [[see:burgle]].
The British verb, which sounds odd to American ears, unlike [[see:burglarize]].
An Anglo-Saxon fortified, walled settlement, found at the end of place names like [[see:Edinburgh]], [[see:Peterborough]] and [[see:Canterbury]], and in [[gave:burglary]].
A place name ending in [[from:burh]].
A place name ending in [[from:burh]].
A place name ending in [[from:burh]].
The pre-Norman word for a burglar; the Normans Latinised its first part, giving [[gave:burglary]].
A legal term for theft from a Latin word for hiring or a mercenary, someone paid to be a bandit; rarely heard in Britain.
An old word meaning a sin, as in prayers, from Latin [[from:transpassare]], to pass beyond; in English, to cross a border; compare French [[same-root:trépasser]].
In French this relative of [[same-root:trespass]] means to die, to pass over.
An Old English word of uncertain root; 19th-century dictionaries said a thief steals without the victim knowing, unlike a [[see:robber]].
In 19th-century dictionaries, one who stole or plundered openly, with the victim aware, unlike the sneakier [[see:thief]].
Related to [[same-root:reaver]] and [[same-root:rover]], and distantly to [[same-root:corrupt]].
Related to [[same-root:rob]].
Related to [[same-root:rob]].
Feels political but literally means to break or destroy, from the [[from:rumpere]] root discussed before; related to [[same-root:rupture]], [[same-root:disrupt]] and distantly [[same-root:rob]].
Came via French, from the same Latin root meaning to burn as [[same-root:ardour]] and [[same-root:ardent]].
Shares a Latin root meaning to burn with [[same-root:arson]].
Shares a Latin root meaning to burn with [[same-root:arson]].
Probably from French [[from:pocher]], to put in a bag, since poachers bagged animals; once romanticised as defiance of the rich, like [[see:Robin Hood]], but not for endangered species.
French for a bag, now also a pocket, the source of [[gave:poke]] and [[gave:pocket]].
A bag or sack, from French [[from:poche]], as in [[see:pig in a poke]].
Buying a pig in a sack without seeing it, which might turn out to be a bad pig or a cat.
From the French for a small bag, related to [[same-root:poche]].
Related to [[same-root:poaching]] game: the white forms a little pocket for the yolk.
Non-subsistence hunting for fun, open only to the wealthy, which made [[see:poaching]] a way to stick it to them; discussed in an earlier episode.
Shot deer in the king's woods, an example of romanticised [[see:poaching]].
From a Latin word meaning to leap or skip; first adventurous pranks, then entertaining crimes like jewel thefts thanks to crime fiction and films.
The act of making things, from the same French source as [[same-root:forge]].
A place where you make things, from the same French source as [[same-root:forgery]].
A non-violent white-collar crime whose Old French origin meant to steal, with senses ranging from torment and destroy to gouge.
Shows the same oddly violent link between money and physical torment as [[see:embezzlement]].
Intensifying per- plus Latin [[from:necare]], to kill, so literally to kill violently; related to [[same-root:innocent]].
Means not harming, related to [[same-root:pernicious]]; Jess says she got it wrong in an earlier episode.
Related to [[same-root:corrupt]].
Related to [[same-root:corrupt]].
From Greek [[from:skandalon]], a stumbling block or trap for an enemy; in the 13th century a moral stumbling block, gossipy by the late 16th; same root as [[same-root:slander]].
From Old French [[from:esclandre]], an inflammatory or false statement, the same source as [[same-root:scandal]] but gaining extra syllables through French.
Sounds like a word [[see:William Shakespeare]] would have invented by adding -ize to [[from:scandal]].
From the Greek for bad or villainous speech; has meant speaking against God or saying anything out of order.
From French [[from:saboter]], to bungle or walk noisily as in clunky wooden shoes; the tale of workers throwing shoes into machinery is probably folk etymology.
Child snatching: first abducting children for forced labour or slavery, mainly on American plantations; the [[see:nap]] part means snatching.
The snatching element in [[see:kidnap]].

Essentially means to snatch; related to [[same-root:rapid]], [[same-root:ravine]], [[same-root:rapt]], [[same-root:rapture]], [[same-root:raptor]] and [[same-root:ravenous]]; unrelated to [[unrelated:rapeseed]].
Related to [[same-root:rape]], from the idea of snatching.
Related to [[same-root:rape]], from the idea of snatching.
Related to [[same-root:rape]], from the idea of snatching.
Related to [[same-root:rape]], from the idea of snatching.
Related to [[same-root:rape]], from the idea of snatching.
Literally being snatched away to heaven, related to [[same-root:rape]].
Means a type of thief, as in the dinosaurs [[see:oviraptor]] and [[see:velociraptor]]; related to [[same-root:rape]].
A dinosaur whose name means egg thief, from [[from:raptor]].
A dinosaur whose name means speedy thief, from [[from:raptor]].
Earth that has been snatched away, related to [[same-root:rape]].
If you're rapt, your attention has been captured; related to [[same-root:rape]].
Related to [[same-root:ravine]] and [[same-root:rape]], and unrelated to [[unrelated:raven]] despite appearances.
Looks related to [[unrelated:ravenous]] but isn't.
The plant behind rapeseed or canola oil, from Latin [[from:rapa]], turnip, unrelated to [[unrelated:rape]] the crime.
A variety of [[see:rapeseed]] gardeners might grow, which sounds worse than it is.
A variety of [[see:rapeseed]] gardeners might grow, which sounds worse than it is.
Basically a noun form of [[from:hoist]]: lifting something big, a bigger theft, like thieves lifting things from pockets.
The verb behind [[gave:heist]].
An old-fashioned word for a criminal, since to lift something is to steal it, as in [[see:shoplifter]].
Shows the stealing sense of lift found in [[see:lifter]].
An old name for a thief, from twigs smeared with sticky lime used to snare birds.
An old name for a thief; to pug at something is to pull or grasp at it.
An old name for a thief, specifically a lock picker, with gilt spelled like gold, suggesting snatching gold.
An old name for a thief, from [[from:niman]], the Old English word for take.
The Old English verb for take, used before take itself, which gave [[gave:nimmer]].
An old name for a thief.
Cockney rhyming slang for thief, still sometimes heard; Rob's parents had a cat called Tea Leaf.
An old word for a thief, apparently from a word meaning to grip or grasp, like [[same-root:cloying]].
A 16th–17th-century word for a thief, referring to [[see:Robin Goodfellow]], the mischievous forest sprite; compare the film [[see:Goodfellas]].
A film about gangsters, much less charming than the old thief sense of [[see:good fellow]].
A mischievous forest sprite mentioned in A Midsummer Night's Dream, the source of [[gave:good fellow]].
Too sweet or too much, apparently from a word meaning to grip or grasp, related to [[same-root:cloyer]].
A dialect word Rob associates with [[see:cloying]].
An old word for a criminal: [[from:wandel]], an old Germanic word for a crime, plus the [[from:-ard]] ending.
An originally intensifying, now pejorative ending for someone who does something too much, as in [[see:braggart]] and [[see:drunkard]].
Someone who brags too much, an example of [[from:-ard]].
Someone who drinks too much, an example of [[from:-ard]].
An old Germanic word for a crime, apparently related to [[same-root:wander]] and [[same-root:Vandals]].
A people who were literally wanderers, related to [[same-root:wander]] and to [[same-root:wandel]], a word for crime.
Related to [[same-root:Vandals]] and [[same-root:wandel]], reflecting a long association of wanderers with crime.
Literally a wanderer, from Latin [[from:vagari]], to wander around.
Seen at different times as romantic or criminal, like [[see:vagabond]].
Named for tramping across the country, and once romanticised.
Of uncertain origin: perhaps the railroad workers' call [[from?:ho boy]], or [[from?:hick]], a word for a loutish, uneducated country person.
A common call to railroad workers and a possible source of [[gave?:hobo]]; it reminds Rob of [[see:hautboy]].
A word for a country person implying loutishness and lack of education, a possible source of [[gave?:hobo]].
The older English name for the [[see:oboe]], an anglicised rendering of French [[from:hautbois]].
An Italian take on French [[from:hautbois]], high wood, because it's a relatively high-pitched wooden instrument.
French haut, high, plus bois, wood, for a high-pitched wooden instrument; the source of [[gave:oboe]] and [[gave:hautboy]].
From Latin [[from:fello]], evildoer, of unclear origin: maybe Frankish for scourger, Latin for poison, or Latin [[from?:fellare]], to suck, as a joke; also once a boil.
A semi-fossil word meaning wicked or cruel, related to [[same-root:felon]], surviving in [[see:one fell swoop]] and [[see:fell beast]].
Coined by [[see:William Shakespeare]] in Macbeth, comparing a family's slaughter to little birds taken by a hawk in one murderous swoop.
A particularly wicked or cruel beast, using the same [[see:fell]].
Uses the semi-fossil [[see:wreak]], which took on the sense of inflicting in the 1800s, with [[see:havoc]].
From Old English for drive out or avenge; extended to mean inflict in the 1800s, notably by [[see:Percy Bysshe Shelley]], who paired it with ruin.
The poet who popularised the inflicting sense of [[see:wreak]] by writing of wreaking ruin upon tyrants.
Originally an Anglo-French war cry ordering soldiers to pillage, hence Mark Antony's "Cry havoc" in [[see:William Shakespeare]]'s Julius Caesar.
Coined [[see:one fell swoop]], used [[see:scandal]] and [[see:havoc]]; the hosts note how many crimes happen in his plays.
Once a punishable crime of lurking at night under a house's eaves to listen in, where rainwater dripped on you; [[from:eavesdrip]] was first a noun.
Also eavesdrop, originally a noun for the concealed area under the eaves where water dripped off, the source of [[gave:eavesdropping]].
An old crime like [[see:kidnap]] but for adult men, abducting them and forcing them into military service.
A petty crime of joining a [[see:skimmington]], an unruly and probably unofficial shaming parade.
A noisy parade humiliating an unfaithful or abusive spouse through the village; also a term for a henpecked husband.
Can be short for convict or confidence artist; conning means gaining someone's confidence to get something out of them, as discussed before.
From German, describing both cheats and giddy people, perhaps from the giddiness of gambling; the theory is murky; compare [[from:Schwindler]].
German for a swindler, behind [[gave:swindle]].
Black for evil plus Middle English mail, rent or tribute: extorting payment like a [[see:racket]]; related to [[same-root:meet]] and [[same-root:meal]], not letters or armour.
The modern word for the kind of extortion originally called [[see:blackmail]].
Ultimately related to the mail in [[same-root:blackmail]].
Related to the mail in [[same-root:blackmail]], implying an appointed time for gathering and eating.
To wrench or twist something out of someone, from Latin [[from:torquere]], to twist, as in [[same-root:distort]] and [[same-root:torque]].
Shares the twisting root of [[same-root:extortion]].
Shares the twisting root of [[same-root:extortion]].
An informer; usually a word for a nose, so someone poking around in business that isn't theirs.
One of the words for informing to the police after being squeezed.
One of the words for informing to the police.
One of the words for informing to the police.
One of the words for informing to the police.
A police informer from the 1800s, probably from a Romani word for nose; not short for narcotic, though the narcotics-agent sense was influenced by [[from:nark]].
The older spelling for a snitch, Victorian prison slang for a policeman's spy, which influenced [[gave:narc]].
Meaning mad, from 18th–19th-century London prison slang made up so the guards couldn't understand.
Meaning clothing, from old London prison slang.
Meaning nose, from old London prison slang.
A policeman, from London prison slang, which gave the more American [[gave:cop]].
More of an Americanism, from the London prison slang [[from:copper]].
To idle or kill time, originally prison slang for sleep; unrelated to [[unrelated:dossier]].
Jess wonders whether it's related to [[unrelated:doss]]; it isn't.
Old prison slang for hands, as in put your dukes up.
Prison slang for lending someone money, as in front me a tenner.
Meaning a gang, from prison slang.
Meaning head, from prison slang.
Originally prison slang for a partner in crime.
Prison slang originally for a sovereign, now meaning a pound.
Prison slang for borrowing something, as in wanting to bite my ear for a shilling.
Prison slang for drunk, now died out, missing from the hosts' earlier list of British words for drunk.
Rhyming slang for boots, heard in the song [[see:My Old Man's a Dustman]].
A song whose dustman calls his hobnail boots [[see:Daisy Roots]]; Rob sings it, Lonnie Donegan-style.
Prison rhyming slang for shouting stop thief.
Prison slang for a burglar.
Prison slang for paying a bribe, like [[equivalent:grease someone's palm]], using [[see:dukes]] for hands.
To pay a bribe, the familiar version of [[equivalent:grease someone's duke]].
The 20th-century gay slang of London, which absorbed prison slang and was heavily influenced by Italian; saved for a future episode.
A police informer, earlier a decoy pigeon tied to a movable stool or perch to lure hawks and other wild birds.
A [[equivalent:fall guy]], perhaps from Italian [[from?:pazzo]], madman or fool, someone not clever enough to avoid being framed.
Somebody who takes the fall for a crime, another word for a [[equivalent:patsy]].
From Leviticus' Yom Kippur rite: one goat sacrificed, the other sent into the wilderness bearing the people's sins; scape is short for [[from:escape]].
Compared to the [[see:scapegoat]]; discussed in an earlier episode.
The original Hebrew term behind [[gave:scapegoat]], related to the name of the demon [[same-root:Azazel]].
Now the name of a demon, related to the Hebrew [[same-root:goat that departs]].
The Latin translation of the Hebrew [[from:goat that departs]], an equivalent of [[equivalent:scapegoat]].
The German equivalent of [[equivalent:scapegoat]].
The Greek equivalent of [[equivalent:scapegoat]].
The French equivalent of [[equivalent:scapegoat]], matching the Latin [[equivalent:caper emissarius]].
Literally to get out of your cape, as if dancing out of a grabbed cape; shortened to [[gave:scape]], as in [[gave:scapegoat]].
A shortened form of [[from:escape]] in [[see:scapegoat]], [[see:scape-grace]] and [[see:scape-gallows]], unrelated to [[unrelated:landscape]].
Not related to [[unrelated:scape]], short for escape.
Someone who has escaped the grace of God, using [[from:scape]].
Someone who deserves hanging but dodges the noose, from [[from:scape]]; Jess's favourite word from the episode.
Literally true said, from Latin; its dict is the same as in [[same-root:dictation]].
Shares the dict, meaning said, of [[same-root:verdict]].
